title: Who shapes global AI rules — and who gets left out?
label: 28 October 2026 · Multilateralism: AI governance
summary: Dr Rachel Adams of the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence explained how AI rule‑making is increasingly contested between wealthier states, China and emerging powers, but many low‑ and middle‑income countries are already writing non‑binding AI frameworks that lack enforcement. She urged stronger, practical multilateral support—training, regional links, and tracking of promises—so the Global South can negotiate fair deals, protect rights and build capabilities.

speakers.label: Dr Rachel Adams
speakers.name: Dr Rachel Adams
speakers.role: Executive Director, Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, University of Cambridge; founder of the Global Center on AI Governance

glossary.definition: A term for lower‑ and middle‑income countries in Africa, Latin America, Asia and elsewhere, often with different priorities from wealthy countries.
Very large cloud and AI companies (e.g. major US and Chinese firms) that provide data centres and computing power.
A group of 20 major economies that meet to coordinate on global economic and political issues.
A United Nations process intended to bring many countries and stakeholders together to discuss AI governance.
World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, a China‑led initiative launched in 2026 to promote AI cooperation.
Training and diplomatic work to help countries negotiate AI rules, access to technology and international partnerships.
An international funding initiative (originating with Canada and Sweden) supporting AI capacity building in developing countries.
UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, which funds international development and diplomacy work.

chapters.title: Who should set AI rules?
chapters.takeaway: Relying only on advanced powers to set AI norms risks leaving many countries behind and creating instability.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourself and tell us whether it's sensible for technologically advanced powers to set global AI rules for everyone.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: I'm Dr Rachel Adams, Executive Director at Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre and founder of the Global Center on AI Governance, which supports Global South governments.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Having only a few advanced countries set norms is risky. Those rules may not suit other countries and can block research and cooperation—GDPR is an example.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: We're in a multipolar world. If only some nations shape AI law, other regions will be left behind and tensions about control and values will grow.

chapters.title: What's happening in the Global South?
chapters.takeaway: Many developing countries are publishing AI frameworks, but most are non‑binding and lack enforcement or resources.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: Do governments in the Global South feel left out, and what do they care about most?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: They do feel excluded from global rule‑making. Our Global Index on Responsible AI shows recent growth: over half of new frameworks come from the Global South.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: But 78% of those frameworks are non‑binding—they show intent but usually lack enforcement, oversight bodies or budgets to implement protections.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Implementation also lags: roughly 45% of Global South frameworks are being implemented versus about 65% in the global North, though many are new.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: The risks countries prioritise differ. Rich countries worry about frontier and existential risks; many Global South concerns are immediate: labour, weak institutions, and data sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Examples: underpaid data‑labelling work with no labour protections, overwhelmed human rights bodies handling complaints about new data centres, and unequal environmental impacts.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Public understanding is low. In South Africa two‑thirds of people we surveyed didn't know what AI was; those who did relied on platforms for information, which affects democratic accountability.

chapters.title: Who is helping and where are the gaps?
chapters.takeaway: There are multiple international initiatives, but coordination, regional tailoring and follow‑through are weak.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: Some say middle‑income countries are a US‑China battleground. Is that how they see it?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: That's a Western framing. African governments don't mainly see themselves as pawns in a binary US‑China contest. They want practical partnerships and agency.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: US influence now often flows through big tech, while China offers accessible open models and training. Both have advantages and limits, depending on local needs.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: On multilateral mechanisms: UNESCO's ethical framework and readiness tool were useful but relied on global indicators that don't always include many countries.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: The UN Global Dialogue is inclusive, but with thousands of short statements it's hard to reach concrete commitments or follow up on promises.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: China's WAICO launched in 2026 emphasised development and training and has some African signatories; it's early to judge its impact.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: The G20 is valuable—South Africa used it well—but global processes need links to regional bodies like the African Union and to national regulators so commitments turn into action.

chapters.title: Diffusion of AI and capacity building
chapters.takeaway: Technology adoption is uneven and many development efforts succeed only when they support local priorities and institutions.

turns.speaker: Lord Darroch of Kew
turns.text: Microsoft found 25% AI use in workplaces in the global North versus 14% in the Global South—how effective have international initiatives been at spreading capability?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Such stats are useful but often model formal economies; they miss informal work common in many countries. Diffusion doesn't automatically mean fair benefits.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: The AI for Development initiative (originating with Canada and Sweden, with FCDO support) has helped universities and projects across Africa, producing useful local innovations.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Successful programmes focus on local priorities, strengthen democratic institutions, and build university capacity—these are long‑term, not quick‑win, investments.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Many funders and tech firms favour fast scaling. But without institution building and citizen engagement, gains aren't sustained or equitable.

chapters.title: What can the UK realistically do?
chapters.takeaway: The UK should use diplomatic tools—training, scholarships, and G20 leadership—rather than only money or infrastructure, to support Global South agency.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: How can the UN processes be shaped so the Global South really buys in? And about WAICO: are its African signatories long‑standing Chinese partners?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: For the UN, make it practical: link global talks to regional bodies, national regulators and funding so commitments become concrete and trackable.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: I can't name the ten WAICO signatories offhand. It's important to study their ties to China, but irrespective of origins, these initiatives matter because they offer political voice and training.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: With the UK's aid cuts and fewer diplomats, is the UK credible in offering meaningful engagement?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Yes—credibility can come from non‑expensive diplomatic tools. The UK should fund AI diplomacy training, use Chevening scholarships, and support university partnerships.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Strengthen institutions in partner countries: competition authorities, data protection agencies, human rights bodies and gender commissions—help them participate fully in global talks.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: The UK has world‑class universities and global diplomatic reach; using those for training diplomats and regulators is high value and relatively low cost.

chapters.title: Top practical recommendations
chapters.takeaway: Make global processes result in tracked, funded action; train diplomats and regulators; use the G20 and UK universities to build Global South agency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What's your top recommendation to the British Government?

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Use the G20 to revive commitments from South Africa's presidency, especially on labour, unequal access to compute and tech's social harms—bring those into concrete follow‑up actions.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Second, the UK should anchor an AI diplomacy programme—train diplomats and regulators from the Global South so they can engage and negotiate effectively.

turns.speaker: Dr Rachel Adams
turns.text: Finally, track commitments across forums. When companies and states pledge training, money or capacity building, there must be a way to see whether resources and training really flow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Dr Adams. We appreciate your time and these concrete suggestions.
